text:
(NewsNation) — Gregory Bovino, who became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration, retired Tuesday, ending an over 30-year career with the U.S. Border Patrol.

But Bovino, who at times faced harsh criticism, including from President Donald Trump, for his handling of immigration enforcement operations that he oversaw in cities like Chicago, Los Angeles and Minneapolis, didn’t leave his post without casting blame on former selected federal officials.

Chief among them were White House border czar Tom Homan and Customs and Border Protection Chief Rodney Scott. On Tuesday, Bovino accused Homan and Scott of “saying nothing” in the wake of the death of a college student in Chicago, who Department of Homeland Security officials said this week was shot and killed by a Venezuelan national who was permitted to remain in the United States after entering illegally in 2023.

The migrant, Jose Medina, was charged with murder this week in the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Sheridan Gorman, a freshman at Loyola University Chicago. Gorman was shot while with friends last week along the Lake Michigan shoreline near Loyola’s campus.

“The Gorman family is burying their daughter this week, and liberal commissioner Rodney Scott and capitulator Tommy Homan say and do nothing, which is how we got in this mess in the first place,” Bovino told NewsNation on Tuesday.

Gregory Bovino refused to back down after being replaced in Minneapolis

Scott, who, along with Homan, was assigned to take over the immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis in the wake of the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, declined to comment on Bovino’s characterization of his actions when contacted Tuesday by NewsNation.

Bovino was relieved as the Border Patrol’s commander-at-large overseeing the Minneapolis operation after President Donald Trump sent Homan to Minnesota. After the deaths of Good and Pretti, Trump suggested that a “softer touch” was likely needed. Trump characterized Bovino as a “pretty out there kind of a guy.”

Bovino returned to the Border Patrol’s El Centro Sector, where he served as sector chief before taking on the title of commander-at-large. Department of Homeland Security officials disputed that Bovino was dismissed from the role, which sources told NewsNation did not exist before Bovino.

Bovino announced earlier this month that he would be retiring from the Border Patrol by the end of March. His departure from the agency came on the same day as Oklahoma Republican Sen. Markwayne Mullin was sworn in as DHS secretary by Trump. Mullin replaces Kristi Noem, who has been reassigned within the Trump administration after Trump fired her earlier this month.

“Those Border Patrol Agents I’ll miss dearly,” Bovino told NewsNation Tuesday. “They are the very best and the most hardcore I know of. Put any mission in front of them, anywhere and it WILL be accomplished. When the Green Team is not around, bad things happen.”

However, Bovino acknowledged to The New York Times in a lengthy profile that appeared Tuesday that he leaves the Border Patrol with a few regrets. Namely, he told the newspaper that not enough arrests of criminal immigrants, who Bovino routinely referred to as “aliens” and who allegedly entered the United States illegally, took place under his watch.

“I mean, we went as hard as we could, but there’s always a creative and innovative solution to catching even more,” Bovino told the newspaper.

Bovino, who, the report indicated, plans to return to his native North Carolina to hunt coyotes in his retirement, did not respond to multiple messages asking for clarification about his comments from NewsNation.

The long-time Border Patrol official referred to his superiors within DHS as “status quo bureaucrats,” including Homan, who was accused by Democrats of accepting a $50,000 bribe, although charges were never filed. In referring to the allegations, Bovino told the Times, “You’re not going to see me talking to anyone for a bag of money.”

Homan did not respond to NewsNation’s request for comment on Bovino’s allegations. The border czar previously told NewsNation that the allegations involving the alleged bribe were “bull—-“. In an interview later Tuesday with NewsNation, Homan took exception to Bovino’s comments about doing nothing about illegal immigration, saying, “I’ve deported more illegal aliens than anybody since the Eisenhower administration.”

Homan called Bovino “a patriot” and thanked him for his service to the United States.

“I mean, anybody who thinks Tom Homan’s soft on immigration is just wrong,” Homan told NewsNation Wednesday. “But look, I appreciate Greg’s service. I appreciate him, you know, putting that badge and gun on every day, so I hope he’s happy in retirement.”

In taking over for Bovino in Minneapolis, Homan told reporters that he was not there for photo opportunities, which The New York Times report indicated that Bovino routinely sought after. In both Minneapolis and Chicago, Bovino was captured on video throwing tear gas canisters at protesters.

His actions in Chicago landed him in front of a federal judge, who accused Bovino of lying repeatedly under oath about his use of force against protesters. In interviews with NewsNation, Bovino said that he and his fellow Border Patrol agents used the minimum amount of nonlethal force in dealing with protesters, who routinely clashed with federal immigration agents and officers under Bovino’s watch.

After being criticized by Judge Sara Ellis last October, Bovino vowed that he would “go harder” and that Border Patrol agents would “turn and burn as we always say here at Operation Midway Blitz … and we’re going to apprehend even more illegal aliens, bad people and bad things here on the streets of Chicago.”

New DHS Secretary Mullin commits to taking new approach in running agency

In his first confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill last week, Mullin, the new DHS secretary, told lawmakers that his goal was to keep DHS from being “the lead story” daily as was often the case under Noem’s leadership.

Mullin stepped back from some of his initial comments about the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti at the hands of federal immigration officers in Minneapolis.

Yet Bovino never backed off from his commitment to the Border Patrol’s “turn and burn” mentality, which he spoke of in numerous interviews with NewsNation in Chicago and Minneapolis. Bovino’s approach drew the ire of elected officials in both cities, including Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and his mayoral counterpart in Minneapolis, Jacob Frey.

Homan committed to meeting with local officials to help lower the emotional temperature in Minneapolis after the two fatal shootings of Minneapolis residents.

Even after being deployed back to El Centro, Bovino never acknowledged any missteps in his leadership style. Homan told reporters that he was not blaming anyone in particular for the change of leadership but repeated that operations could be run “smarter,” seemingly referring to a change from the way Noem and Bovino had overseen the Minneapolis mission.

But in speaking to The New York Times, Bovino said, “We wanted total border domination. When you use terms like that, perhaps it scares some of the weaker-minded people. Domination. I want you to dominate that border. I’m not going to ‘control’ it. We’re going to dominate the hell out of that damn place.”

Home

Daily News

DOJ guts program helping immigrants receive…

Immigration Law

DOJ guts program helping immigrants receive affordable legal representation

The Department of Justice has gutted a program that helps low-income and indigent immigrants receive competent and affordable legal representation, according to sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

The Recognition & Accreditation Program is part of the DOJ’s Executive Office for Immigration Review. The program accredits nonattorneys who work for largely faith-based legal advocacy organizations, such as Catholic Charities and Jewish Family Services, so they are authorized to help immigrants with legal matters, including naturalization petitions and representation in immigration court, according to a story by CBS News.

DOJ attorneys operating the program were reassigned to work in immigration courts last week. The remaining two support staffers have no legal authority to approve or renew accreditation applications, sources with direct knowledge said, according to CBS News.

The program accredits more than 2,600 nonattorneys across more than 900 recognized programs, according to CBS News.
